analysis.one_liner: Taxes the unrealized gains of wealthy people who renounce U.S. citizenship to escape taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2002 with 5 Democratic sponsors, sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, and never received a hearing, vote, or action before Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: When a wealthy person gives up U.S. citizenship, current rules make it hard to collect the taxes on gains they built up while American. This bill would treat all their property as sold the day before they renounce, taxing the gains then — with a $600,000 cushion for smaller holders — and would put a tax on gifts and inheritances above $10,000 that expatriates leave to people in the United States. It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and died there without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary American taxpayers generally, since people who renounce citizenship to escape taxes on built-up gains would have to settle up with the IRS before leaving, and heirs in the U.S. receiving large gifts from expatriates would owe tax on them rather than receiving them tax-free.

how_it_helps.text: Treats all property of a 'covered expatriate' as sold at fair market value the day before expatriation, so unrealized gains are taxed instead of escaping U.S. tax permanently, with a $600,000 exclusion for smaller gains.

Imposes a tax, paid by the recipient, on covered gifts and bequests above $10,000 per year from expatriates to U.S. citizens and residents, closing the route of renouncing citizenship and then transferring wealth back tax-free.
Applies to long-term residents as well as citizens, and requires anyone deferring the tax to post adequate security and waive treaty rights that would block collection.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy individuals who renounce U.S. citizenship or end long-term U.S. residency — they would owe tax on unrealized gains (above $600,000) at the moment of departure — and U.S. recipients of gifts or inheritances over $10,000 from expatriates, who would pay the estate-tax rate on the amount received.

drawbacks.text: The mark-to-market rule taxes gains on property that was never actually sold, forcing expatriates to pay tax on paper gains in illiquid assets — such as a private business or real estate — before they have received any cash from them.

The tax on covered gifts and bequests applies to any U.S. recipient of more than $10,000 per year from an expatriate and is paid by the recipient, which could reach ordinary family members inheriting from a relative who gave up citizenship, not only the wealthy.
The bill adds substantial complexity: trust interests, deferred tax accounts, and valuation rules would all require new regulations and compliance burdens.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is between closing a real gap — people renouncing citizenship to escape tax on large built-up gains — and imposing a departure tax on assets never sold, which is hard on holders of illiquid wealth. The $600,000 exclusion and carve-outs for retirement plans and U.S. real property focus the burden on larger holdings, but the $10,000 gift-tax threshold is low enough to reach modest inheritances from an expatriate relative.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Rangel, joined by Rep. Richard Gephardt, introduced the bill on June 6, 2002, to prevent use of renouncing U.S. citizenship as a device for avoiding U.S. taxes.
Four other House Democrats cosponsored it; no Republicans did.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and no further action of any kind was taken on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy individuals who renounce citizenship to avoid U.S. taxes, and anyone who benefits from that practice, are better off because the bill died without a vote; ordinary taxpayers continue to cover the difference.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy people who renounce to avoid taxes

for.name: Rep. Charles B. Rangel
for.role: U.S. Representative, NY-15; senior Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, with introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: Rep. Richard Gephardt
for.what_they_did: Joined Rangel as the bill's co-introducer.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 6, 2002, and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or report — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would tax unrealized gains at the moment of renouncing citizenship and tax their gifts and bequests to U.S. recipients, ending the ability to leave the U.S. tax system with built-up gains intact.

industries.industry: International tax and trust planning services
industries.note: Advisers who structure citizenship renunciations and offshore trust arrangements to preserve gains would face a regime of deferred tax accounts, security requirements, and trustee liability that curtails the value of those services.
